newsitem.title: USA: Clinton not considering intervening in UPS dispute.
newsitem.headline: Clinton not considering intervening in UPS dispute.

text.p: President Clinton was not considering intervening in a labour dispute that threatened to shut down United Parcel Service, an administration official said on Thursday.

Teamsters union members have threatened to walk off the job at midnight and paralyse UPS, which moves some 12 million packages a day. The White House official, who asked not to be identified, said that the only way Clinton could intervene in the dispute would be to invoke a law that has not been used since the 1950s.

Clinton would have to use the cumbersome and time-consuming Taft-Hartley law to order a mediation board to settle the dispute, the official said. The law gives the government wide powers to prevent and settle labour disputes, including imposing a cooling-off period and setting collective bargaining procedures.

But the official said it could be invoked only when a strike in an industry would have a significant impact on the American economy. It has not been used since a steel industry strike in the the 1950s, he added.
President Clinton used a different law, the Railway Labour Act, to intervene in a strike by American Airline pilots earlier this year.
Senior presidential adviser, Bruce Lindsey, met with officials from both United Parcel Service and the Teamsters union earlier on Thursday, the White House said.
